title: William D. Ford Federal Direct Loan (Direct Loan) Program
summary:
The U.S. Department of Education finalized a rule that narrows which employers qualify for the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program. Starting July 1, 2026, organizations found to have a “substantial illegal purpose” will no longer qualify, and employees will stop earning credit toward forgiveness from that point forward.

The rule spells out what “substantial illegal purpose” means in plain terms. Examples include breaking federal immigration laws, supporting terrorism or using violence to influence federal policy, performing unlawful medical procedures on minors, transporting children across state lines to cut off parental rights in violation of law, aiding illegal discrimination, or repeatedly violating certain state laws such as trespassing, disorderly conduct, vandalism, public nuisance, or blocking highways. The Department says it will act only on evidence and will not penalize lawful advocacy or protected speech. It will use a “more likely than not” standard, give employers notice and a chance to respond, and treat earlier qualifying work by borrowers as fully credited.

Who benefits: Borrowers who work for law‑abiding public service employers should see clearer rules, faster notification when an employer’s status changes, and an updated public list of qualifying employers. Taxpayers may benefit from fewer improper subsidies—government estimates show about $1.6 billion in savings over ten years—while the Department expects only a small number of employers (fewer than ten a year) to be affected. The process also allows employers to regain eligibility after ten years or sooner with an approved corrective plan.

Who may be negatively affected: Borrowers whose employers are later ruled ineligible will stop earning new credit unless they switch to another qualifying employer. This could be especially hard for people with limited job options, such as those in rural areas or bound by long training contracts. Some nonprofits, advocacy groups, and small organizations worry the standards could be applied inconsistently or chill lawful work, and they point to added administrative work to document compliance. The Department counters that the rule is not retroactive, protects constitutional rights, relies on evidence rather than politics, and keeps credit borrowers already earned.

In short, the change aims to tighten program integrity and protect public funds, while raising difficult tradeoffs for employees of organizations that fall on the wrong side of the new line.
